title: PredNext: Temporal Prediction for Unsupervised Spiking Networks
one_liner: Spiking neural networks learn video representations without labels by predicting what the network will see in future video frames.
lead: Spiking neural networks (brains-like models with time-based signals) are good at learning from video, but today's unsupervised methods are shallow and unstable. PredNext adds a prediction module: while the main network watches a video, an extra module guesses what the network will perceive in the next moment and the next chunk. This prediction task forces the network to build stable, useful representations without any labeled data.

problem.h2: Why today's unsupervised spiking networks fail
paras: Spiking neural networks are special: they work more like brains, with signals that fire or not at each time step, and they naturally handle time-based data like video. But teaching them from unlabeled video is hard. Today's methods are mostly shallow (only a few layers), and they only use local rules (changes happen in one place at a time), so they cannot learn to connect events that happen far apart in time.

A beginner might try: just force the network to make the same features for the same object no matter when it appears in the video. But the paper shows this backfires—it actually makes the network worse, because the penalty for small changes overwhelms the real learning signal.

callout.b: The problem: shallow networks + no long-range time learning.
callout.html: Spiking networks need a way to learn deep, stable time-aware features from unlabeled video.

steps.b: Watch two views of the same video
steps.text: The spiking network sees the same video sequence twice (maybe from different cameras or crops).
For each frame, the network builds a feature list (a set of numbers describing what it sees).
A small prediction head guesses: given frame 3's features, what will frame 4's features look like?
A second predictor guesses: given frames 1-5's features, what will frames 6-10's features look like?
The network learns to minimize how far its guesses miss. Features that are good for prediction become stable and useful.

paras: The paper adds a separate prediction module that sits on top of the spiking network. This module learns to guess future features, but it does not change the network's weights directly. Instead, the prediction task acts as a teaching signal: features that lead to good predictions get reinforced, features that are noisy or inconsistent do not. This is different from directly penalizing inconsistency (which the paper shows fails).
object.object: prediction module attached to feature stream

hidden.h2: Temporal Feature Consistency: The Hidden Quantity
hidden.name: temporal feature consistency error
paras: Temporal feature consistency error measures how much a feature changes when you look at the same object at different times in a video. Imagine a cat walking across the screen: at frame 10 the network builds a feature list for cat-ness, and at frame 15 the same cat appears again. If the features for that cat are very different, the consistency error is high (bad). If they are nearly identical, consistency error is low (good).

The paper estimates this by computing the average cosine distance (a way to measure how far apart two lists of numbers are) between features from different frames of the same video. The network does not know it is being measured this way; instead, the prediction task indirectly optimizes for consistency because predicting next-frame features is easier when current features are stable.

heat.caption: Darker cells show larger feature drift between adjacent frames. Highlighted cells show where features should stay most similar.

reads.html: Consistency error is how much features wiggle over time for the same object.
Consistency error is the average cosine distance between representations from different timesteps of the same video.

paras: The core trick: if features for an object jump around randomly, predicting the next frame becomes a guessing game—your prediction will miss. But if features for the same object stay stable over time, you can predict reliably. So the network faces a choice: build wild, noisy features and fail at prediction, or build calm, consistent features and succeed. The prediction loss (how much your guess misses) pulls the network toward consistency without explicitly penalizing it.

Why is this better than direct consistency penalties? Because forcing features to be identical at every frame is too strong—sometimes the network legitimately needs to update what it sees (shadows move, the camera pans). The prediction task allows gradual, genuine change while suppressing noise because the predictor is designed to track slow drifts. When the network changes a feature by a small, deliberate amount, the predictor can track it and still guess the next frame correctly, so the loss stays low. When the network jitters randomly instead, the predictor's guesses miss wildly and the loss shoots up. Since the network wants to minimize loss, it learns to keep features steady during jitter and adjust them only when necessary. This teaches the network that short-term stability is valuable without locking it into incorrect representations.

stages.s: Current frame features from spiking network
Step prediction head: guess next-frame features
Clip prediction head: guess next-chunk features
Compute loss between guess and actual future
Network adjusts weights to reduce loss on next epoch

math.note: When features stay stable over time, the predictor nails its guess and loss drops. Noisy features give high loss, so the network learns to reduce noise.

charts.title: Baseline (no PredNext)
charts.note: Without prediction guidance, features drift apart and the network struggles.

charts.title: With PredNext
charts.note: Prediction forces consistency because stable features are easier to predict. Better consistency also improves accuracy: the features the network built work better for classification. Transfer improves because features based on real temporal patterns are more general than those based on random noise.

items.html: If you directly penalize feature drift (say, make frame-to-frame features identical), performance crashes. Strong penalties cut accuracy from 72 to 60 percent because the network is locked into stale, incorrect representations.

If you predict too far into the future (10 steps ahead when objects move fast), the task becomes impossible and the network learns nothing. Too close (1 step), and the guidance is too weak. The paper shows prediction steps of 3–5 frames work best.

If the spiking network has only 2–3 layers, the prediction module has no varied features to work with because shallow networks build only low-level, simple patterns (like edge detectors). There is nothing complex enough to predict, so the loss signal is too weak to guide learning. The method requires deep architectures (8+ layers) to work because deeper networks build richer, more predictable hierarchies.

Predicting within a single view of the video is weaker than predicting across two different crops or camera angles. The cross-view constraint forces the network to learn view-invariant features, not camera-specific artifacts.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simple spiking network on a small video dataset (e.g., UCF101 subset with 10 action classes). Train it unsupervised: show it unlabeled videos and apply the prediction loss. After 50 epochs, freeze the network and fine-tune a linear classifier on top of the learned features using just 1 percent labeled data. Compare: (1) the network trained without PredNext, (2) the network with forced consistency penalty, (3) the network with PredNext. Measure both accuracy on the test set and temporal consistency error (cosine distance between features from the same action at different times).
demo.metric_eq: test_accuracy = (correct_predictions) / (total_test_videos); consistency_error = avg(1 - cosine_similarity(feature_t, feature_t+k) for all videos and k in 1..5)
demo.closing: The demo must show: PredNext achieves the highest accuracy and lowest consistency error, and forced penalties actually make things worse—proving that prediction guidance is the right tool, not direct constraints.
